name: Tumour mutational burden (TMB)
summary: Tumour mutational burden quantifies somatic coding mutations per megabase and serves as an imperfect surrogate for neoantigen load; high TMB has been associated with benefit from immune checkpoint inhibitors, but assay harmonisation and thresholds remain challenging.
biology: Tumours with many somatic mutations, such as smoking-associated NSCLC and SCLC, generate more potential neoantigens that may be presented on MHC and recognised by T cells. TMB is independent of PD-L1 expression. Mismatch-repair deficiency and POLE mutations produce very high TMB.
alterations: Hypermutation from mismatch-repair deficiency or POLE/POLD1 mutation

testing.specimen: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumour tissue or plasma ctDNA
testing.notes: Panel-derived TMB depends on panel size, bioinformatic pipeline, germline filtering and tumour purity; values from different assays are not directly interchangeable.

predictiveRelevance: High TMB supports tissue-agnostic use of pembrolizumab in some jurisdictions and correlated with benefit from nivolumab plus ipilimumab in NSCLC exploratory analyses; however, TMB is not routinely used to select first-line immunotherapy in NSCLC and has limited predictive value in SCLC and breast cancer outside hypermutated tumours.
resistance: Low TMB and low neoantigen clonality associated with reduced immunotherapy benefit
